sections.title: Steering Model Control Systems Using Sinusoids

scenes.title: Planning Toolbox
scenes.brief: Top-down parking lot: a blue cart with lime arrows forward/back and a coral ✖ sideways. A gold parking spot sits beside it. Beat 1: a holonomic planner draws a straight slate-dashed line sideways into the spot; the cart refuses and the line flashes coral. Beat 2: a cost meter (effort, length, time) and an orange throttle pinned at its stops, switching sides at orange tick marks (bang-bang). Beat 3: a branching tree of constant moves fans out from the cart (m branches per level, count m^d ticking up), leaves land near but not on the gold spot. Beat 4: three canonical Lego moves (turn-in-place loop, drive, turn) snap together to reach the spot. Beat 5: a chapter map of tiles (sinusoids, Fourier, chained form, optimal, piecewise constant, finger rolling) each lighting when hovered.

scenes.title: Circles Make Height
scenes.brief: A 3D box: the floor is the (q1,q2) plane, the vertical axis is q3. Two orange joystick knobs push a blue bead around the floor; a pink shadow trail draws its floor path while the bead rises or sinks by the signed area swept (teal fill inside the loop, area readout = height). Beat 3 animates the optimal inputs as an orange arrow spinning at constant length on a dial (u(t)=e^{Λt}u0): the floor path is a perfect circle and a cost bar compares it with drawn squares and ellipses of equal area (circle wins). Beat 4 adds more knobs: m floor axes and a so(m) grid of heights, each driven by a pair of knobs spinning at harmonics 1,2,…; Beat 5 is the recipe: first slide the bead straight to its floor target, then trace a circle of the right area to lift it to the gold height.

scenes.title: Beat Frequencies
scenes.brief: Five stacked strip-charts (q1, q2, q12, q121, q122), each a teal wave over one period with its net drift shown as a gold bar at the end. Two orange tone dials pick the frequency of u1 and u2 (1×, 2×, 3× base). A spectrum bar under each row shows which frequencies the state contains (sums and differences of its parents, drawn as colored ticks); a lime ✓ lights only when a zero-frequency tick appears, and that row alone ends displaced. A Jacobi triangle of three bracket arrows that cancel to zero explains why some rows are tied together (purple link).
beats: 🎯 nudge one state at a time

scenes.title: Chained Form
scenes.brief: A vertical chain of n beads (q1…qn). Bead q2 is pulled by orange knob u2; each lower bead moves at a speed equal to the bead above it times the master knob u1 (a slider). Beat 2: a ladder of bracket arrows ad^k g1 g2 lights one new rung (coordinate axis) per bracket, alternating sign. Beat 3: u1 = a·sin(2πt), u2 = b·cos(2πkt) as two orange oscillators; each bead shows a spectrum dial whose dominant frequency drops by one per link until bead k+2 hits zero frequency (gold). Beat 5: drag a and b; a gold readout shows the net jump (a/4π)^k·b/k! matching the simulated RK4 result while all upper beads return home (lime rings).
beats: ⛓️ each link copies the one before

scenes.title: Fourier Steering
scenes.brief: Left: a hopping robot in flight (blue body, orange hip angle ψ and leg length l). Right: a car (blue) with orange steering wheel. Beat 1: wiggle hip and leg in a sine/cosine pair; the body angle α creeps each cycle; repeat to cartwheel 2π. Beat 2: a Fourier bar chart of f(l(t)) shows β1, β2, …; only the first harmonic bar glows gold because it lines up with u1, the others integrate away (teal fades). Beat 3: car coordinates z=(x, φ, sin θ, y) laid beside a pure chain; the coral difference shrinks for small angles. Beat 4: the three-phase car maneuver A, B, C plays out with live Lissajous plots (x,φ two loops; x,θ one loop; x,y open curve that lifts y to gold).

scenes.title: Become a Chain
scenes.brief: Two panels: left the original system with curved blue flow lines of g1, g2; right the same motion in straightened z-coordinates where the flow lines become the stiff chain staircase. A morph slider blends the coordinate grid from curved to straight. Beat 2: nested translucent sheets Δ2 ⊂ Δ1 ⊂ Δ0 (each flat = involutive, lime; a twisted one turns coral). Beat 3: two height maps h1, h2 as colored contour lines: h1 contours stay parallel to Δ1 sheets and climb exactly 1 per unit along g1; h2 contours hug Δ2. Beat 4: a car whose x, y, θ, φ readouts become z1…z4 and the chain steering of the previous scene drives it.

scenes.title: Cheapest Steering
scenes.brief: Main canvas: a state point moving under orange inputs u with a gold target; a coral effort meter integrates |u|². Beat 2: a purple costate arrow p rides along; the Hamiltonian is a landscape and the input arrow always points to make p·g as negative as possible (u = −pᵀg). Beat 3: the input vector u is drawn on a dial; its tip stays on a circle of fixed radius while it turns (norm readout frozen). Beat 4: for Engel’s system the turning angle α behaves like a swinging pendulum (α̈ ∝ sin α) with an energy bar; elliptic-function wave shown. Beat 5: Ritz: a mixer board of Fourier-coefficient sliders per input; a cost readout = coefficient energy + γ·miss distance; gradient/Newton steps animate the sliders until the endpoint lands on gold.

scenes.title: Piecewise Steering
scenes.brief: Beat 1: a flow along one vector field drawn as a train of small straight steps converging to a curve (e^{tg}). Beat 2: a bookshelf of Philip Hall basis fields: shelf 1 holds g1, g2 (orange), shelf 2 [g1,g2], shelf 3 the double brackets (taller shelves are bracket depth); for nilpotent systems the shelves stop. Beat 3: every shelf gets a ghostly fictitious knob v_j; the Chen–Fliess–Sussmann coordinates h_j fill bars as you push the ghost knobs. Beat 4: a box loop (u1, u2, −u1, −u2 for √ε each) traced by a blue cart; the gap between start and end equals ε along the bracket direction, with a faint leak along the next shelf; an eight-leg loop with ∛ε isolates the deeper shelf. Beat 5: for non-nilpotent systems the shelf goes on forever; repeated corrections halve the distance to gold each pass.

scenes.title: Finger Walk
scenes.brief: A three-fingered hand (orange joints, pink tips) holds a slate box fixed in place. Beat 2: a null-space slider moves the fingers while the box stays still (box motion readout locked at 0, lime). Beat 3: zoom on one ball-shaped fingertip on a flat face: five readouts (contact on finger, contact on face, contact angle) drawn as a chain. Beat 4: run sinusoidal inputs; the finger-contact plot traces a closed figure-eight (pink returns home) while the face-contact dot (teal) slides down the face to a gold mark.

scenes.title: Geometric Phase
scenes.brief: A blue ball of adjustable radius rolls on a slate table without slipping; its contact point draws a pink curve on the ball and a teal curve on the table. Beat 2: draw any closed loop on the ball: the ball comes back to the same contact spot but twisted about the vertical by an angle Δψ, and a gold cap area readout on the unit sphere equals the twist (radius slider changes nothing). Beat 3: the four-leg path A→B→C→D→A on the table (legs x, π/2, π/2, x) moves the contact spot along the ball’s equator by distance l = 2(x − atan(2x/π)); drag l and x is solved live. Beat 4: the same area-equals-turn rule on a falling cat, a satellite spinning reaction wheels, and a paramecium with beating cilia.
beats: 🌐 roll a ball on the table
🟦 a square on the table moves the spot

scenes.title: Steering Recap
scenes.brief: A shelf of six tool cards, each a thumbnail of the chapter scene it summarizes (circle loop, chain with sinusoids, conversion morph, constant-norm dial, box loop, rolling ball). Clicking a card replays a 3-second loop of that scene. Beat 2: a horizontal timeline of colored dots for the key ideas (classical nonholonomic mechanics, constructive controllability for mobile robots and rolling fingers, sinusoid steering, optimal-control structure, Ritz numerics, car-with-trailers parking), linked to the tools they produced.

pages.summary: Planning for nonholonomic systems must respect velocity constraints and avoid obstacles, which ordinary planners ignore.

atoms.idea: Chapter 8 title: planning motions for systems with nonholonomic constraints.

Paths must satisfy the velocity constraints ω_i(q)q̇ = 0 and also miss obstacles (for rolling fingers: no finger–finger or finger–object collision). Standard planners assume any direction in configuration space is reachable, so their paths break nonholonomic constraints; dedicated methods are needed.
atoms.feynman: A shopping cart can roll forward and back and turn, but its wheels refuse to slide sideways. A map app that draws a line straight sideways into the parking spot is useless for it: you need a plan the wheels can actually follow.
atoms.visual: Top-down: blue cart, lime forward/back arrows, coral ✖ on the sideways arrow, slate obstacles, gold parking spot to the cart’s side. A slate-dashed straight path snaps in; press ▶ and the cart’s wheels lock, the path flashes coral. Toggle "nonholonomic" and a curvy lime path appears that the cart can follow.

atoms.idea: Section 8.1 Introduction: overview of the general approaches and chapter plan.
Page number.

pages.summary: Three families of planners: optimal control (often bang-bang), piecewise-constant input search, and nilpotent-system methods using the BCH formula.

atoms.idea: Optimal control picks, among all feasible trajectories, the one minimizing a cost functional such as path length, control energy, or travel time.
atoms.feynman: Many routes get you home; you choose the one that uses the least gas, or the shortest, or the fastest — the "price tag" decides the route.
atoms.visual: Several candidate lime paths from the cart to the gold spot, each with a coral cost bar beside it (toggle cost: length / effort / time). The cheapest path thickens and turns gold as the cost type changes.

atoms.idea: With bounded inputs it is natural to minimize time. For convex input sets the time-optimal inputs usually sit at their limits (bang-bang), switching between extreme values at some (possibly infinitely many) instants; planning reduces to choosing switch times and the extreme values between them.
atoms.feynman: To win a go-kart race you hold the pedal flat and steer fully left or fully right — never halfway. The only decisions are when to flip.
atoms.visual: Orange throttle and steering sliders snap only to their end stops; a timeline below shows orange tick marks at switch instants. Drag a tick: the cart’s path re-bends and a time readout updates; the fastest arrangement makes the readout turn gold.

atoms.idea: A naive piecewise-constant planner applies every sequence of discretized constant inputs over fixed time slices, building a tree with m^d nodes after d steps; memory explodes, and the goal is generally reached only approximately, so post-processing is needed.
atoms.feynman: Imagine trying every combination of "left, straight, right" for 10 seconds each: after a few moves you have thousands of possible places, and none is exactly your parking spot.
atoms.visual: From the blue cart, a fan of lime branches grows level by level (one branch per input choice); a counter shows m^d nodes ballooning. Leaves are teal dots; the nearest one to the gold spot glows but leaves a coral miss distance.

atoms.idea: Lafferriere and Sussmann give a general piecewise-constant method for nilpotent systems (all brackets beyond order k vanish), built on the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula; for non-nilpotent systems it at least halves the distance to a nearby goal, so repeating it on small segments converges.
atoms.feynman: Like parallel parking by repeating a small wiggle: each wiggle gets you at least halfway closer to the curb, so a few wiggles put you right there.
atoms.visual: A cart repeats a box-shaped wiggle; a coral distance bar to the gold spot halves after each wiggle (1, ½, ¼ …) on a log scale, converging. A toggle "nilpotent" makes it land exactly in one shot.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Canonical paths stitch special maneuvers together; the chapter outline runs from model systems to general methods to finger repositioning.

atoms.idea: Canonical-path planners pick a family of parameterized maneuvers (e.g. a pure net rotation of a car, or a straight drive) and compose them to reach any configuration; such families are problem-specific, sometimes derived from closed-form optimal paths, and were used for a spherical fingertip rolling on an object.
atoms.feynman: Parking with a handful of practiced moves: "turn on the spot", "drive straight", "turn again". Any parking job is a mix of those three Lego bricks.
atoms.visual: Three Lego bricks (turn-loop, straight, turn-loop) in blue; drag them onto a timeline. The cart executes them in order and ends on the gold spot; a knob per brick sets its angle/length.

atoms.idea: Section 2 steers canonical "model" driftless systems q̇ = Σ g_i(q)u_i (Eq 8.1); for first-order systems the optimal inputs are sinusoids, which motivates sinusoidal steering of higher-order models and leads to chained-form systems.
atoms.feynman: Learn to ride on training wheels first: a perfectly simple toy system shows the trick (wiggle in circles) before you try a real bike.
atoms.visual: Chapter map: six tiles; the first tile (a circle loop lifting a bead) glows and a lime arrow points to a chain-of-beads tile.

atoms.idea: Section 3 extends sinusoids to non-model systems by Fourier analysis, asks when a system can be converted to chained form, and approximates optimal inputs with a Ritz method.
atoms.feynman: Once you can ride the toy, you learn how to tweak the trick for a real car whose steering is a bit bent.
atoms.visual: Map tiles 2–4 light in turn: a Fourier bar chart, a morphing coordinate grid, a mixer board of sliders.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Outline ends with piecewise-constant steering and finger repositioning; Section 2 introduces Brockett’s first-order model system Eq (8.2).

atoms.idea: Remaining outline: piecewise-constant inputs for the general problem, then Section 4 applies these tools plus geometric "canonical trajectory" reasoning to sliding fingertips across a held object.
atoms.feynman: Last stops on the tour: steering with step-like pushes, then a robot hand that walks its fingertips across a cup without letting go.
atoms.visual: Map tiles 5–6 light: a box-shaped loop and a hand rolling a ball-tip across a box face.

atoms.idea: Section 8.2 Steering model control systems using sinusoids.

Model systems are canonical forms that, though they look unrelated to Chapter 7 examples, capture them. Brockett’s optimal-steering results motivate sinusoids at integer-related frequencies; the section starts with degree-two systems of growth vector (m, m(m+1)/2), then chained forms.
atoms.feynman: Like learning music with a metronome: pure tones at 1×, 2×, 3× the beat are the clean building blocks every song is made of.
atoms.visual: Two orange oscillators labeled 1× and 2× ticking in time; a blue bead in a 3D box rises a notch each time the oscillators complete a cycle.

atoms.idea: Section 8.2.1 First-order controllable systems: Brockett's system.
A first-order controllable system: the input fields g_i together with all first brackets [g_j,g_k], j<k, are independent and span the tangent space, which forces n = m + m(m−1)/2 = m(m+1)/2.
atoms.feynman: With two knobs you can move in two directions directly, and wiggling them in a loop gives you exactly one more — so 2 knobs give 3 directions. With 3 knobs you get 3 + 3 = 6.
atoms.visual: A counter panel: m orange knob icons; beneath, m lime arrows plus one teal bracket arrow per knob pair (drawn as a small loop icon between two knobs). Total = m(m+1)/2 updates as you add knobs.

atoms.label: Eq (8.2)
atoms.idea: Brockett’s system with m = 2, n = 3: q̇1 = u1, q̇2 = u2, q̇3 = q1u2 − q2u1.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a toy on a table with two fingers (x and y) while a counter measures how much area your finger path has swept: going around a loop counter-clockwise winds the counter up.
atoms.visual: Two orange knobs move the blue bead on the floor; the bead’s height q3 rises at the rate q1u2 − q2u1 (twice the swept area). A pink floor trail plus teal swept-area fill.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Brockett’s fields have bracket (0,0,2); the least-squares steering problem is posed and its Euler–Lagrange equations show a constant multiplier and rotating inputs.

atoms.idea: g1 = (1,0,−q2), g2 = (0,1,q1), and [g1,g2] = (0,0,2): the system is maximally nonholonomic, degree 2, growth vector (2,3).
atoms.feynman: Go east a bit, north a bit, west, south: you return over the same floor spot but the counter has gone up — the leftover is the "third direction".
atoms.visual: Bracket demo: the bead traces a tiny square on the floor (orange segments g1, g2, −g1, −g2); at the end a gold vertical arrow shows the net lift = 2 × area.

atoms.idea: Goal: steer Eq 8.2 from q0 at t=0 to qf at t=1 while minimizing the energy ∫₀¹ |u|² dt.
atoms.feynman: Get the toy to the right spot and height while tiring your fingers as little as possible.
atoms.visual: Gold target bead; a coral effort meter fills as ∫|u|² accumulates during the drive; try different loops and compare the final meter.

atoms.idea: Since q̇i = ui, the third equation becomes the constraint q̇3 = q1q̇2 − q2q̇1, and the cost integrand is q̇1² + q̇2²; adjoin the constraint with multiplier λ(t) to get L = q̇1² + q̇2² + λ(q̇3 − q1q̇2 + q2q̇1).
atoms.feynman: A rule you must obey becomes a price you pay: the multiplier λ is the fine per unit of breaking the rule, tuned so you never want to break it.
atoms.visual: Equation tokens colored: orange q̇ terms (effort), purple λ·(constraint) term (constraint force). A purple spring between the bead and the allowed surface stays slack when the rule is met.

atoms.idea: Stationary trajectories satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equations of this augmented Lagrangian, the same equations as in mechanics because dynamics itself comes from a least-action principle; λ(t) is fixed by the constraint.
atoms.feynman: A ball rolling in a bowl "chooses" its path to minimize action; our cheapest steering path obeys exactly the same kind of rule.
atoms.visual: Side-by-side: a ball in a bowl (left) and the steering bead (right), both obeying d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q = 0; the shared equation is shown in ∑ layer with tokens colored by picture.

atoms.label: Eq (8.3)
atoms.idea: Euler–Lagrange equations: q̈1 + λq̇2 = 0, q̈2 − λq̇1 = 0, λ̇ = 0, so λ is constant.
atoms.feynman: A charged particle in a constant magnetic field: its velocity just turns at a fixed rate — it goes in circles.
atoms.visual: The bead’s velocity arrow (orange) turns at a constant rate λ while keeping length; a λ readout stays frozen (lime).

atoms.idea: Optimal inputs obey u̇ = Λu with Λ = [[0,−λ],[λ,0]] skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: A merry-go-round turning at a steady speed: anything riding on it rotates, never stretches.
atoms.visual: An orange input arrow on a dial rotating at constant angular speed; the 2×2 Λ matrix shown as a pure rotation generator acting on the dial grid.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Optimal inputs are rotations of u(0); returning (q1,q2) home forces λ = 2nπ, the cheapest is one full circle with |u0|² = 2πa; the m-input generalization lives on R^m × so(m).

atoms.idea: Because Λ is skew with constant λ, u(t) = e^{Λt}u(0): cosine/sine pairs at frequency λ.
atoms.feynman: A clock hand sweeping steadily: its x and y shadows are a cosine and a sine.
atoms.visual: The rotating orange arrow casts two shadows on side strip-charts: a cosine (x) and sine (y) wave drawn live.

atoms.idea: Since q1, q2 are directly steerable, the interesting task is (0,0,0) → (0,0,a). Integrating, (q1,q2)(t) = (e^{Λt} − I)Λ⁻¹u(0).
atoms.feynman: To raise the toy without moving it on the table, your finger must draw a loop that ends where it began.
atoms.visual: Bead starts at the origin; gold target directly above at height a. The floor trail is a circle passing through the origin; its center and radius follow from u(0) and λ.

atoms.idea: Returning to q1=q2=0 at t=1 requires e^{Λ} = I, so λ = 2nπ; then q3(1) = −|u(0)|²/λ = a.
atoms.feynman: The loop has to close, so the clock hand must make a whole number of turns; the height gained is the area wrapped.
atoms.visual: A λ slider snaps only to multiples of 2π (lime ticks); off-tick values leave a coral gap between path end and start. Height readout = −|u0|²/λ.

atoms.idea: Cost = |u(0)|² = −λa, minimized by n = −1: one circle, |u(0)|² = 2πa, with arbitrary direction of u(0); the optimal input is a sine/cosine pair at 2π/T.
atoms.feynman: Of all fences enclosing the same garden area, the circle uses the least fence (and the least running). Go around once, not twice.
atoms.visual: Draw any closed loop with the same area: a coral effort bar compares it to the circle (lime, shortest). Toggle n = 1, 2, 3 turns: smaller circles stacked, more effort.

atoms.label: Eq (8.4)
atoms.idea: m-input generalization: q̇i = ui and q̇ij = qiuj − qjui for i<j — one height per pair of knobs.
atoms.feynman: With three fingers pushing a toy in 3D, each pair of fingers has its own area counter: xy, xz, yz.
atoms.visual: m floor axes; a triangular grid of height counters (one per knob pair) beside the bead; each counter rises with the area swept in its pair-plane.

atoms.label: Eq (8.5)
atoms.idea: Compactly on R^m × so(m): q̇ = u, Ẏ = quᵀ − uqᵀ, with Y skew-symmetric collecting the pair areas.
atoms.feynman: All the area counters fit in one antisymmetric table: the xy counter is minus the yx counter.
atoms.visual: An m×m grid of colored cells; above the diagonal teal, below the mirrored value with opposite sign; cells fill as the bead moves.

atoms.idea: Euler–Lagrange: q̈ − Λq̇ = 0, Λ̇ = 0 with Λ ∈ so(m) the multiplier matrix.
atoms.feynman: Same merry-go-round, but now in more dimensions: the velocity spins in several planes at once.
atoms.visual: Velocity arrow in m-D shown as m/2 independent dials each turning at its own constant rate.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: u(t) = e^{Λt}u(0) in SO(m); Brockett: optimal loops use harmonics 2π, 4π, …; Algorithm 1 steers base states then pair-areas; Section 2.2 starts second-order systems.

atoms.idea: Again Λ is constant and u(t) = e^{Λt}u(0) with e^{Λt} a rotation in SO(m).
atoms.feynman: The input arrow is just being spun around; its length never changes.
atoms.visual: Dial with orange arrow in m-D; a length readout stays fixed (lime).

atoms.idea: Brockett: steering q from 0 back to 0 while Y goes 0 → given nonsingular Y(1) (m even) needs m/2 sinusoids at frequencies 2π, 2·2π, …, (m/2)·2π; for odd m with rank m−1, (m−1)/2 sinusoids at 2π … ((m−1)/2)·2π.
atoms.feynman: A band where each pair of players hums its own note, one octave-step higher than the last: 1×, 2×, 3× the base beat.
atoms.visual: m/2 dials spinning at speeds 1, 2, 3 (orange); a spectrum bar shows exactly these lines (gold), and the so(m) grid fills to the gold target pattern.

atoms.idea: The proof is skipped; the fact motivates a simple steering algorithm for Eq 8.4.
atoms.feynman: You don’t need to know why the band plays those notes to use them.
atoms.visual: A greyed "proof" card flips to show the two-step recipe card.

atoms.label: Algorithm 1
atoms.idea: Steering first-order canonical systems: (1) drive the qi to their targets with any input, ignoring the qij; (2) apply integrally related sinusoids chosen so that the qij reach their targets while the qi return to where they were.
atoms.feynman: Slide the toy to the right spot first, then draw a closed loop to wind the counter to the right number — the loop ends where it started, so the spot doesn’t change.
atoms.visual: Two-stage play button: stage 1 a straight orange drag to the gold floor spot; stage 2 a circle (or harmonic loops) lifting the bead to the gold height; floor readouts stay lime during stage 2.

atoms.idea: The steps go by order: directly controlled states first, then the first-bracket directions.
atoms.feynman: Fix the easy things first, then the tricky sideways ones.
atoms.visual: Stage indicator: rung 0 (lime) then rung 1 (teal) on a two-step ladder.

atoms.idea: Section 8.2.2 Second-order controllable systems.

atoms.label: Eq (8.6)
atoms.idea: When one level of brackets is not enough, add states driven by second-level products: q̇i = ui, q̇ij = qiuj, q̇ijk = qijuk (up to the Jacobi identity).
atoms.feynman: Area counters of area counters: a counter that winds up when you loop while the first counter is already high.
atoms.visual: Three tiers of beads: tier 0 driven by knobs, tier 1 by products of tier 0 and knobs, tier 2 by tier 1 times knobs; tiers drawn as a pyramid.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The Jacobi identity ties some second-order states together; Algorithm 2 steers second-order model systems with sinusoids whose frequency sums and differences hit zero.

atoms.idea: Because [gi,[gj,gk]] + [gk,[gi,gj]] + [gj,[gk,gi]] = 0, not every q_ijk is independently controllable; e.g. q231 − q132 is a fixed function of lower states (q1q23 − q2q13).
atoms.feynman: Three kids on a triangular seesaw: if two tilt, the third is forced. You can’t set all three on your own.
atoms.visual: Jacobi triangle: three teal bracket arrows head-to-tail that close into a loop (sum = 0, lime ✓). Two second-order bead counters linked by a purple chain: move one and the other follows.

atoms.idea: At most (m+1)m(m−1)/3 of the q_ijk are controllable (counting argument from Chapter 7, Exercise 17).
atoms.feynman: Count the truly free counters after crossing out the ones the seesaw rule forces.
atoms.visual: A grid of m³ candidate cells; cells forced by Jacobi grey out in purple; a counter shows the survivors = (m+1)m(m−1)/3 as you change m.

atoms.idea: For these systems the multipliers are no longer constant; for m = 2 the optimal inputs are elliptic functions (Brockett–Dai). Still, Algorithm 1 can be extended.
atoms.feynman: The perfect move becomes a lopsided swing instead of a steady circle — hard to compute, so we settle for a good-enough recipe.
atoms.visual: Ghost of an elliptic-function wave (purple, uneven) next to a clean sinusoid (orange); a toggle chooses the "good enough" sinusoid.

atoms.label: Algorithm 2
atoms.idea: Steering second-order model systems: (1) set the qi (others drift); (2) set the qij with integrally related sinusoids — products of inputs at ωi, ωj contain ωi ± ωj, and a zero component gives net motion; (3) use a second sinusoid set with ωi ± ωj ≠ 0 but a zero component in ωi + ωj + ωk, moving the earlier states in closed loops and only q_ijk net.
atoms.feynman: Two singers humming close notes make a slow "wah-wah" beat (the difference). Choose notes so that the beat vanishes exactly at the level you want to change — only that counter creeps.
atoms.visual: Strip-charts for q1, q2, q12, q121, q122 with spectrum ticks per row (sums/differences of parent ticks). Orange dials pick ω1, ω2; the row whose spectrum contains a zero tick lights gold and ends displaced; all other rows end on their start (lime rings).

atoms.idea: Step 2 is identical to Algorithm 1; Step 3 is messy in general but simple for concrete systems, e.g. m = 2.
atoms.feynman: The general rulebook is thick, but for a two-knob toy you can just do it by hand.
atoms.visual: Switch to the m = 2 preset: five rows appear, ready for step 3.
atoms.beat: 🎯 nudge one state at a time

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: For m = 2, sin 2πt against cos 4πt moves q121 alone (by −a²b/16π²) and the swapped pair moves q122 alone (by a²b/32π²); chained-form systems introduced.

atoms.feynman: A five-bead abacus where lower beads move only when the bead above is off-center and you push.
atoms.visual: Five beads in a pyramid (tier 0: q1,q2; tier 1: q12; tier 2: q121,q122), each linked by arrows from its driver.

atoms.idea: Section 8.2.3 Higher-order systems: chained form systems.

General higher-order canonical forms exist but are hard to steer with sinusoids; the chained systems are a special class that sinusoids at integer frequencies do steer. They are dual to the Goursat normal form, and many systems convert to them.
atoms.feynman: A train: the engine pulls car 1, car 1 pulls car 2, and so on — each car only follows the one in front. That simple pulling chain is easy to drive with rhythm.
atoms.visual: A vertical chain of beads hanging from an orange knob, each linked to the one above; a faint "Goursat" twin chain mirrored in purple shows the dual picture.

atoms.label: Eq (8.7)
atoms.idea: One-chain system: q̇1 = u1, q̇2 = u2, q̇3 = q2u1, q̇4 = q3u1, …, q̇n = q_{n−1}u1.
atoms.feynman: A car pulling trailers: the first input drives, the second steers, and each trailer’s heading creeps toward the one ahead only while you drive.
atoms.visual: Bead chain: q2 pulled by knob u2; each lower bead’s speed = (bead above) × u1, drawn as a lime belt whose speed shows u1.

atoms.idea: Call Eq 8.7 the one-chain system. Iterated brackets: ad_{g1}g2 = [g1,g2], ad^k_{g1}g2 = [g1, ad^{k−1}_{g1}g2].
atoms.feynman: Wiggling the steering inside a drive-loop, then wiggling that inside another drive-loop: each nesting reaches one trailer further.
atoms.visual: A nested-loop icon: loop inside loop inside loop; each nesting level highlights the next bead in the chain.

atoms.label: Lemma 8.1
atoms.idea: For the chain fields, ad^k_{g1}g2 = (−1)^k e_{k+2}: a single nonzero entry in slot k+2 with alternating sign.
atoms.feynman: Each extra nesting of the wiggle moves exactly the next trailer — first backwards, then forwards, alternating.
atoms.visual: Ladder of coordinate axes e3, e4, …; pressing "+bracket" lights the next rung with an arrow pointing up (+) or down (−) alternately; all other entries shown as zero dots.

atoms.idea: Proof by induction, starting from the first two brackets because the first level is irregular.
atoms.feynman: Check the first two rungs by hand, then show "if a rung works, the next one does too".

pages.summary: Proof of Lemma 8.1, controllability of the one-chain (Prop 8.2), and Algorithm 3: u1 = a sin 2πt, u2 = b cos 2πkt moves only q_{k+2}.

atoms.idea: Base cases: [g1,g2] = −e3 and [g1,[g1,g2]] = +e4.
atoms.feynman: First two dominoes: one wiggle shifts trailer 1 backward, a wiggle-inside-a-wiggle shifts trailer 2 forward.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 1: compute brackets numerically by tiny flows; arrows appear at e3 (coral, down) and e4 (lime, up).

atoms.idea: Inductive step: bracketing (−1)^k e_{k+2} with g1 gives (−1)^{k+1} e_{k+3}, since only the q_{k+2} entry of g1 depends on that coordinate.
atoms.feynman: If one domino falls, it knocks the next one, with the sign flipping each time.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 2: domino row of rungs; each falls onto the next, flipping arrow direction.

atoms.label: Prop 8.2
atoms.idea: The one-chain system is completely nonholonomic, hence controllable.
atoms.feynman: With the trailer trick, you can put every trailer anywhere.
atoms.visual: All n rungs lit lime = full rank; a gold ✓ appears.

atoms.idea: g1, g2 and ad^i_{g1}g2 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−2 give n independent fields by Lemma 8.1.
atoms.feynman: Count the directions you can push: n of them, all different — enough.
atoms.visual: Rank meter fills to n as rungs light.

atoms.idea: Heuristic: with u1 = sin 2πt and u2 = cos 2πkt, q3 carries frequency 2π(k−1), q4 2π(k−2), …, and q_{k+2} gets a zero-frequency part, so it drifts while earlier states return.
atoms.feynman: Each trailer hears the beat of the one before, slowed by one notch. The k-th trailer down hears a beat that has slowed to a stop — a steady push — so it alone moves.
atoms.visual: Each bead has a spectrum dial; play the inputs and watch the dominant tick step down 1 per link until a gold zero tick appears at bead k+2.

atoms.label: Algorithm 3
atoms.idea: Steering chained form: (1) set q1, q2; (2) for each q_{k+2}, k ≥ 1, apply u1 = a sin 2πt, u2 = b cos 2πkt with (a/4π)^k b/k! equal to the needed change.
atoms.feynman: Fix the engine and first car, then for each trailer down the line play the matching rhythm once to nudge just that trailer.
atoms.visual: Algorithm runner: step buttons per bead; each step plays the oscillators (orange) for one period; the targeted bead jumps to gold, the rest end where they started.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Prop 8.3: Algorithm 3 works — only zero-frequency terms survive, giving q_{k+2} a jump of (a/4π)^k b/k!; Section 3 begins on general steering.

atoms.label: Prop 8.3
atoms.idea: Algorithm 3 can steer the one-chain system to any configuration.
atoms.feynman: The trailer-rhythm recipe can park every trailer anywhere.
atoms.visual: Random gold target configuration; run the algorithm; every bead lands on gold.

atoms.idea: Constructive proof: products of sinusoids split into sums at frequencies shifted by ±1 step; a state changes over a period only via its zero-frequency component, so only the lowest frequency per state matters.
atoms.feynman: Over a full swing, anything that wiggles averages out; only a steady push leaves a mark.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 1: each bead’s signal decomposed into colored sinusoid strands; strands with nonzero frequency fade to grey after one period, the zero-frequency strand (gold) remains.

atoms.idea: Integrating from the origin: q1 ∝ (1 − cos 2πt), q2 ∝ sin 2πkt, q3 has frequencies 2π(k±1), q4’s lowest is 2π(k−2), …, until q_{k+2} contains a sin² 2πt term whose average is ½, giving linear growth.
atoms.feynman: Pass the rhythm down a line of people; each one slows it a notch; the last one is just steadily walking.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 2: a waterfall plot: rows = beads, horizontal = frequency; the lit ticks march left one column per row until hitting zero at row k+2.

atoms.idea: So q_{k+2}(1) = q_{k+2}(0) + (a/4π)^k b/k! and earlier states are periodic; nonzero initial conditions only add terms like q_{i−1}(0)u1 that integrate to zero.
atoms.feynman: The payout depends on how hard you wiggle each knob; starting from a different spot only adds extra wobbles that cancel.
atoms.visual: Payout readout: formula value vs simulated jump side by side; randomize the start: extra coral wobble lines appear but their net bars are zero.

Real systems rarely appear exactly in model form, so more general techniques are needed.
atoms.feynman: Real bicycles aren’t textbook toys; you need to adapt the trick.
atoms.visual: A real car silhouette fades in over the ideal bead chain, with small coral mismatches.

pages.summary: Fourier techniques: the hopping robot in flight becomes a near-chain system after a Taylor expansion and coordinate change; sinusoids then steer its body angle.

atoms.idea: This section covers planning methods for general nonholonomic systems.
atoms.feynman: Now we take the toy trick out into the real world.
atoms.visual: Section banner tile: a hopper and a car side by side, each with a small orange oscillator icon.

atoms.idea: Section 8.3.1 Fourier techniques.
Integer-frequency sinusoid steering can be adapted with basic Fourier analysis to systems outside the model classes; two Chapter 7 examples illustrate it.
atoms.feynman: If your instrument is slightly out of tune, you listen to which overtones it produces and adjust how loud you play.
atoms.visual: A Fourier bar chart icon slides in next to the oscillator pair.

atoms.label: Ex 8.1, Eq (8.9)
atoms.idea: Hopping robot in flight: ψ̇ = u1 (hip), l̇ = u2 (leg extension), θ̇ = −m(l+d)²/(I + m(l+d)²) · u1 (body rotates to conserve angular momentum).
atoms.feynman: A diver in mid-air: swinging the arms one way twists the body the other way; stretching or tucking changes how much it twists.
atoms.visual: Side view: blue body, orange hip angle ψ and leg-length l sliders; swinging the leg counter-rotates the body (θ readout). Angular momentum bar stays at 0 (lime).

atoms.idea: Taylor-expand in l: θ̇ ≈ −md²/(md²+I) ψ̇ − 2mdI/(md²+I)² · l u1 + O(l²)u1. With α = θ + md²/(md²+I) ψ the system becomes ψ̇ = u1, l̇ = u2, α̇ = f(l)u1.
atoms.feynman: Measure the body angle relative to the leg’s average twist: then only the stretch-while-swinging part changes it, like a chain link.
atoms.visual: Coordinate swap animation: θ dial morphs into α dial; the formula α̇ = f(l)u1 appears with f plotted as a teal curve, its straight tangent at 0 overlaid in blue.

atoms.idea: Dropping the higher-order terms gives a 3-state chain, which justifies using the chain algorithm on the exact system: set ψ and l first, then use u1 = a1 sin 2πt, u2 = a2 cos 2πt for one period to move α while ψ and l return; l(t) = (a2/2π) sin 2πt.
atoms.feynman: Swing the leg in a circle (forward-out, back-in): each loop the body turns a bit, and the leg ends where it started.
atoms.visual: Hopper animation: leg tip traces a closed orange loop in (ψ, l) space; α dial ticks forward each loop; ψ and l readouts return home (lime).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Only the first Fourier coefficient of f(l(t)) produces net body rotation: Δα = a1β1/2; the kinematic car becomes a near-chain via z = (x, φ, sin θ, y).

atoms.idea: Expand f((a2/2π) sin 2πt) = β1 sin 2πt + β2 sin 4πt + …; over one period only the β1 term survives against u1: Δα = a1β1/2. β1 depends on a2, so solve numerically for (a1,a2); a full mid-air cartwheel is Δα = 2π.
atoms.feynman: Push a swing in time with its own rhythm and it goes higher; pushes at the wrong rhythm cancel out. Only the matching harmonic pays.
atoms.visual: Fourier bar chart of f(l(t)) (teal bars β1, β2, …); multiply by u1’s sine: only β1’s bar turns gold and feeds a Δα meter. Root-finder adjusts a1, a2 until the hopper completes a 2π flip.

atoms.label: Ex 8.2
atoms.idea: Kinematic front-wheel-drive car (Eq 7.14): ẋ = cos θ u1, ẏ = sin θ u1, θ̇ = (tan φ / l) u1, φ̇ = u2; u1 alone moves no single state directly.
atoms.feynman: A real car: the gas pedal moves you along your heading, the steering wheel turns the front wheels, and turning only happens while you roll.
atoms.visual: Top-down blue car with orange steering wheel and gas pedal; heading θ and steering φ drawn as arcs; no sideways motion (coral ✖).

atoms.idea: With z1 = x, z2 = φ, z3 = sin θ, z4 = y and v1 = cos θ u1, v2 = u2: ż1 = v1, ż2 = v2, ż3 = (tan z2 / l) v1, ż4 = z3/√(1−z3²) v1; the linear parts match a one-chain and Fourier analysis absorbs the rest.
atoms.feynman: For small angles a car is just a chain of trailers: steering angle → heading → sideways position.
atoms.visual: Two columns: car states and chain beads; lime links where they agree; coral mismatch bars grow with steering angle (drag φ).

atoms.idea: Figure 8.1 shows the car maneuver in phases: A sets x and φ with constant inputs; B uses a sine/cosine to fix θ while returning the others; C uses u1 = a1 sin 4πt, u2 = a2 sin 2πt …
atoms.feynman: Three moves: drive into place, wiggle to straighten the heading, then a double wiggle to slide sideways.
atoms.visual: Phase timeline A | B | C below the car; each phase highlights its orange input waveform.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 8.1 shows the three-phase car maneuver; its Lissajous loops reveal Lie-bracket motions as rectified harmonics. Section 3.2 asks when a system can be converted to chained form.

atoms.label: Fig 8.1
atoms.idea: Car path from (x,y,θ,φ) = (−5, 1, 0.05, 1) to (0, 0.5, 0, 0): plots of φ, y, θ versus x and inputs versus time, segmented into A, B, C.
atoms.feynman: Like a dance with three parts — a walk, a twirl, a figure-eight — each part fixes one thing and leaves the rest as they were.
atoms.visual: Four live plots: φ vs x (two loops in C), θ vs x (one loop in C), y vs x (open curve that drops y to gold), and u1,u2 vs time with A/B/C bands; a blue car moves along.

atoms.idea: In phase C, the (x,φ) Lissajous curve has two loops, (x,θ) one loop, and (x,y) is open — the net y gain. Bracket motions are rectified harmonic periodic motions, with the harmonic ratio set by the bracket order.
atoms.feynman: A ratchet turns back-and-forth jiggling into steady turning; here a 2:1 jiggle of two knobs ratchets the car sideways.
atoms.visual: Lissajous panel: closed loops drawn in lime (states that return), the open curve in gold (the state that moves); a frequency-ratio dial (1:1, 2:1, 3:1) shows which depth of bracket it reaches.

atoms.idea: Section 8.3.2 Conversion to chained form.
Question: can a change of inputs and a nonlinear change of coordinates turn a given nonholonomic system into a model (chained) form?
atoms.feynman: Is this crooked road secretly a straight road seen through warped glasses?
atoms.visual: Morph slider: curved coordinate grid with blue flow lines; sliding toward "straight" warps the grid until the flow becomes the chain staircase.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Sufficient conditions for two-input systems to become a one-chain: nested distributions of constant rank and involutive, plus functions h1, h2 defining the new coordinates by Lie derivatives.

atoms.idea: Find an input transform v = β(q)u and a diffeomorphism z = φ(q) so that the system is chained in (z, v).
atoms.feynman: Rename your knobs and redraw your map so that the machine behaves like the simple chain toy.
atoms.visual: Two panels: original (q, u) and transformed (z, v); colored knob relabeling arrows from u to v (orange), grid map q → z.

atoms.idea: Necessary and sufficient conditions exist but are heavy; for two inputs with g1, g2 independent there are simpler sufficient conditions for one-chain form.
atoms.feynman: There is a complete rulebook, but for two knobs a short checklist is enough.
atoms.visual: Checklist card with three boxes appears on the side of the morph panel.

atoms.idea: Conditions: Δ0 = span{g1, g2, ad g2, …, ad^{n−2} g2}, Δ1 = span{g2, ad g2, …, ad^{n−2} g2}, Δ2 = span{g2, …, ad^{n−3} g2} (ad = ad_{g1}) must each have constant rank and be involutive.
atoms.feynman: Stacks of flat sheets of paper: each family of allowed directions must lie flat (no twist) so it can be stacked into layers.
atoms.visual: Nested translucent sheet families Δ2 ⊂ Δ1 ⊂ Δ0; an involutivity test brackets two in-sheet arrows: if the result stays in the sheet, sheet glows lime, else coral twist.

atoms.idea: Need h1 with dh1·Δ1 = 0 and dh1·g1 = 1, and h2 independent of h1 with dh2·Δ2 = 0. Frobenius guarantees functions annihilating the nested involutive Δ2 ⊂ Δ1; the extra normalization dh1·g1 = 1 is the real condition.
atoms.feynman: Find a height map that stays flat along all sheets of one stack but climbs exactly one step for every unit you push the go-pedal.
atoms.visual: Contour lines of h1 (gold) lie along Δ1 sheets; a step counter along a g1 flow line increases by exactly 1 per unit time; h2 contours (teal) lie along Δ2.

atoms.idea: New coordinates z1 = h1, z2 = L_{g1}^{n−2}h2, …, z_{n−1} = L_{g1}h2, z_n = h2, with v1 = u1 and v2 = (L_{g1}^{n−1}h2)u1 + (L_{g2}L_{g1}^{n−2}h2)u2, give ż1 = v1, ż2 = v2, ż_k = z_{k−1}v1.
atoms.feynman: Measure h2, then how fast it changes along the go-pedal, then how fast that changes… each derivative becomes the next trailer in the chain.
atoms.visual: A column of repeated "rate of change along g1" operators turns h2 into a stack of beads z_n, z_{n−1}, …, z2; play the system and the beads follow the chain rule exactly.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Example 8.3 converts the kinematic car to a one-chain with h1 = x, h2 = y; Section 3.3 poses least-squares optimal steering with Lagrange multipliers.

atoms.idea: The procedure is illustrated on the kinematic car.
atoms.feynman: Now try the warped-glasses trick on a real car.
atoms.visual: Car icon slides into the morph panel.

atoms.label: Ex 8.3
atoms.idea: Write the car as ẋ = u1, ẏ = tan θ u1, θ̇ = (tan φ / l) u1, φ̇ = u2. With h1 = x, h2 = y the conditions hold, giving z1 = x, z2 = curvature-like (tan φ / l) times a power of sec θ, z3 = tan θ, z4 = y, and v from an explicit input map.
atoms.feynman: Measure the car by: how far along the road, how sharply it is turning, its slope, and how far sideways — that list behaves exactly like a trailer chain.
atoms.visual: Car panel with readouts x, y, θ, φ morphing into z1…z4 beads; drive with chain inputs v1, v2 and the car parks sideways into a gold slot.

atoms.idea: Section 8.3.3 Optimal steering of nonholonomic systems.
Least-squares optimal control: steer q̇ = Σ g_i(q)u_i from q0 to qf in unit time minimizing ½∫₀¹ |u|² dt.
atoms.feynman: Get there on time while burning the least fuel.
atoms.visual: State point with gold target; coral effort meter integrating ½|u|²; candidate paths with costs.

atoms.idea: Informal derivation; existence assumed via Chow’s theorem (bracket rank n everywhere). Constraints are adjoined with a multiplier function p(t) ∈ Rⁿ.
atoms.feynman: Promise first that the trip is possible (enough knob combinations), then attach a fine for each moment you break the rules.
atoms.visual: Bracket rank bar full (lime) unlocks the optimizer; a purple multiplier arrow p appears riding on the state.

atoms.label: Eq (8.10)
atoms.idea: J(q,p,u) = ∫₀¹ [½uᵀu − pᵀ(q̇ − Σ g_i u_i)] dt.
atoms.feynman: Total bill = fuel used + fines for any mismatch between where you move and where the knobs allow.
atoms.visual: Equation tokens colored: orange ½uᵀu, purple p, blue g_i; a stacked bar shows fuel vs fine (fine stays at 0 on valid paths).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The Hamiltonian, first variation, and stationarity give u_i = −pᵀg_i, the optimal Hamiltonian H*, and Hamilton’s equations; Prop 8.4 begins.

atoms.label: Eq (8.11)
atoms.idea: Hamiltonian H(q,p,u) = ½uᵀu + pᵀ Σ g_i(q)u_i.
atoms.feynman: A compass p tells you how much each direction is worth; H trades fuel against progress in valuable directions.
atoms.visual: Purple costate arrow p and blue field arrows g_i; an H landscape over the input plane (bowl) with its bottom marked gold.

atoms.idea: Integrating by parts: J = −pᵀq |₀¹ + ∫₀¹ (H + ṗᵀq) dt.
atoms.feynman: Move the derivative from one factor to the other, paying only boundary terms.
atoms.visual: Two shaded areas swapping: the area under −pᵀq̇ equals boundary bars minus area under ṗᵀq.

atoms.label: Eq (8.12)
atoms.idea: First variation δJ in δu, δq must vanish: ṗ = −∂H/∂q and ∂H/∂u = 0.
atoms.feynman: At the bottom of a valley, small steps in any direction don’t change your height.
atoms.visual: Wiggle the optimal input path with a small teal perturbation; a δJ readout stays ~0 (lime) on the optimum and is nonzero elsewhere.

atoms.label: Eqs (8.13)–(8.14)
atoms.idea: Stationarity gives u_i = −pᵀg_i(q); substituting, H*(q,p) = −½ Σ (pᵀg_i)².
atoms.feynman: Push each knob in proportion to how much the compass values that knob’s direction.
atoms.visual: Each orange input bar equals minus the projection of purple p onto blue g_i (drawn as shadow lengths).

atoms.label: Eq (8.15)
atoms.idea: Optimal trajectories obey Hamilton’s equations q̇ = ∂H*/∂p, ṗ = −∂H*/∂q, with boundary conditions q(0) = q0, q(1) = qf.
atoms.feynman: Like a planet: position and momentum evolve together, and you choose the starting kick so you land on the target.
atoms.visual: Phase-space pair: state point (blue) and costate arrow (purple) evolving by RK4; drag the initial p to shoot the endpoint onto gold (shooting).

atoms.label: Prop 8.4
atoms.idea: Constant norm of optimal controls (statement begins): for least-squares steering of q̇ = Σ g_i u_i satisfying the rank condition …
atoms.feynman: Claim: the best driver always presses the controls equally hard.
atoms.visual: Input dial appears with a radius readout ready.

atoms.idea: Footnote: the variation means perturbing u by δu and tracking induced changes δp, δH.
atoms.feynman: Nudge the plan slightly and watch what else shifts.
atoms.visual: Small teal δu perturbation curve overlaid on the optimal input.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Prop 8.4: optimal inputs have constant norm, because u̇ = Ω(q,p)u with Ω skew; consequences for other costs and Engel’s system.

atoms.idea: … the optimal input has constant norm: |u(t)|² = |u(0)|² for all t ∈ [0,1].
atoms.feynman: The best plan keeps the gas pedal at a steady pressure; only the mix of directions changes.
atoms.visual: Input dial: orange tip stays on a fixed lime circle while turning.

atoms.idea: Differentiate u_i = −pᵀg_i, substitute ṗ from Hamilton’s equations; the terms combine into u̇_i = Σ_j pᵀ[g_i,g_j]u_j.
atoms.feynman: How the input changes depends only on how much the compass values each "wiggle direction" (bracket).
atoms.visual: Staircase step 1: product-rule split of d/dt(pᵀg_i) into two colored terms; they merge into a bracket arrow [g_i,g_j] projected on p.

atoms.label: Eq (8.16)
atoms.idea: In matrix form u̇ = Ω(q,p)u with Ω_ij = pᵀ[g_i,g_j], a skew-symmetric matrix in so(m).
atoms.feynman: A spinning turntable can only rotate what sits on it, never stretch it.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 2: Ω shown as a grid with mirrored opposite-sign entries; acting on the input arrow only rotates it.

atoms.label: Eq (8.17)
atoms.idea: The time-varying linear ODE has solution u(t) = U(t)u(0) with U(t) ∈ SO(m) (Exercise 6), so the norm is constant.
atoms.feynman: Rotations never change length.
atoms.visual: Staircase step 3: the input arrow carried by a rotating frame; length readout frozen (lime).

atoms.idea: Constant norm means the same input also solves problems with monotone transformations of the integrand, e.g. ∫√(uᵀu) dt, and some minimum-time problems (Exercise 8); it also helps solve Engel’s system.
atoms.feynman: If you always drive at the same speed, the cheapest-fuel route is also the shortest route and, after scaling, the fastest.
atoms.visual: Three cost meters (energy, length, time) for the same path; ranking of candidates is identical across meters.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Engel’s system (growth (2,3,4)): optimal inputs are (r sin α, r cos α) with α obeying a pendulum equation, solved by elliptic integrals.

atoms.label: Ex 8.4
atoms.idea: Engel’s system: q̇1 = u1, q̇2 = u2, q̇3 = q1u2 − q2u1, q̇4 = q1²u2; growth vector (2,3,4); [g1,g2] = (0,0,2,2q1).
atoms.feynman: Like Brockett’s toy but with an extra counter that weighs the swept area by how far east you are.
atoms.visual: Bead with two counters: plain area (q3) and east-weighted area (q4) shown as a gradient-colored fill.

atoms.label: Eq (8.18)
atoms.idea: Specializing Eq 8.16: u̇1 = 2(p3 + q1p4)u2, u̇2 = −2(p3 + q1p4)u1, so u = r(sin α, cos α) with r constant.
atoms.feynman: The pedal pressure is fixed; only the steering direction turns, at a speed that depends on where you are.
atoms.visual: Input dial with fixed radius r; turning speed readout α̇ varies with q1 (color-coded east–west).

atoms.idea: H* = −½(p1 − q2p3)² − ½(p2 + q1p3 + q1²p4)² does not depend on q3, q4, so p3, p4 are constant, and α̈ = 2p4 r sin α.
atoms.feynman: The turning angle swings exactly like a pendulum.
atoms.visual: Side-by-side: pendulum bob (blue) and the input dial angle α moving in lockstep.

atoms.label: Eq (8.19)
atoms.idea: Energy integral: α̇² = b − 2δ cos α (δ = 2p4r); if b − 2|δ| > 0, α̇ = c√(1 − k sin²(α/2)), integrated by an elliptic integral of the first kind.
atoms.feynman: A pendulum that has enough energy to go over the top keeps spinning, fast at the bottom and slow at the top; the timing follows a special "elliptic" curve.
atoms.visual: Energy bar for the α-pendulum (stays fixed, lime); α(t) plotted as a non-uniform staircase wave (elliptic function) vs a uniform sine.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Engel’s optimal inputs are elliptic functions; the Ritz method approximates optimal inputs with a truncated Fourier basis and a penalized cost; Section 3.4 introduces piecewise-constant steering.

atoms.idea: So the optimal inputs for Engel’s system are elliptic functions.
atoms.feynman: The perfect swing is a lopsided pendulum rhythm, not a pure tone.
atoms.visual: Elliptic wave locked in gold on the input strip.

atoms.idea: Exact least-squares steering is usually intractable; the Ritz method restricts each input to a truncated orthonormal trigonometric basis of L²[0,1] (1, √2 cos 2kπt, √2 sin 2kπt), u_i = Σ_{k≤N} α_ik ψ_k.
atoms.feynman: Instead of drawing any wiggle you like, you build it from a fixed set of piano notes and only choose their volumes.
atoms.visual: Mixer board: N+1 sliders per input (orange), each a Fourier coefficient; the waveform above updates as the sum of colored basis waves.

atoms.label: Eqs (8.20)–(8.21)
atoms.idea: Choose coefficients to minimize J = ½(Σ|α_i|² + γ|q(1) − qf|²): effort plus a penalty γ for missing the goal; large N and γ should give a low-cost input that nearly reaches qf.
atoms.feynman: Score = how loudly you played + a big fine times how far you missed. Make the fine big enough and you’ll hit the target.
atoms.visual: Cost readout split into coral effort and purple miss-penalty bars; a γ slider; the endpoint (pink) and the gold goal with the miss distance drawn.

atoms.idea: The finite-dimensional problem can be solved by many methods, e.g. a modified Newton iteration (implemented in a published package).
atoms.feynman: Now it’s a normal "find the lowest point" puzzle with a few dials.
atoms.visual: Press ▶: Newton/gradient steps move the sliders; a ball rolls down the cost bowl; the endpoint lands on gold.

atoms.idea: Section 8.3.4 Steering with piecewise constant inputs.
Outline of Lafferriere and Sussmann’s method for general nonholonomic systems.
atoms.feynman: Steering with step-like pushes: hold a knob, switch, hold another.
atoms.visual: Input strip changes to a staircase (piecewise-constant) waveform.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: For nilpotent systems, flows are formal exponentials of vector fields; the Chen–Fliess formula writes every reachable flow as a product of exponentials along a Philip Hall basis.

atoms.idea: The method needs the controllability Lie algebra to be nilpotent of order k (brackets with more than k factors vanish); its first step builds a canonical system using formal power series in vector fields.
atoms.feynman: Wiggles inside wiggles eventually stop doing anything new — after k levels the toy has no more hidden directions, so the list of moves is finite.
atoms.visual: Bracket-depth tower: levels 1…k colored, level k+1 drawn as empty slate outlines (all zero).

atoms.idea: The flow of g_i for time t is written as a formal exponential e^{tg_i}(q), with the formal series I + t g_i + (t²/2!) g_i² + … treated as a map Rⁿ → Rⁿ (justification of powers deferred).
atoms.feynman: Following a river current for t seconds is "doing a tiny step over and over" — the same recipe as compound interest.
atoms.visual: A dot follows a blue flow line; n small straight steps (orange) converge to the curved flow as n grows (slider n).

atoms.idea: Take a Philip Hall basis B1, …, Bs of the nilpotent controllability Lie algebra (brackets up to order k, respecting skew-symmetry and Jacobi); brackets are formal polynomials, e.g. [g1,g2] = g1g2 − g2g1.
atoms.feynman: A tidy bookshelf listing every distinct move once: plain moves, wiggles, wiggles-of-wiggles — no duplicates, no moves that the seesaw rule makes redundant.
atoms.visual: Bookshelf: shelf 1 orange g1, g2; shelf 2 teal [g1,g2]; shelf 3 double brackets; duplicates and Jacobi-dependent books fade purple and fall off.

atoms.label: Eq (8.22)
atoms.idea: Chen–Fliess: every flow of q̇ = Σ g_i u_i from q has the form S_t = e^{h_s(t)B_s} ⋯ e^{h_1(t)B_1}(q).
atoms.feynman: Any dance you can do is the same as doing each basic move from the bookshelf once, for the right amount of time, in a fixed order.
atoms.visual: A product-of-exponentials ribbon: one colored segment per basis book, lengths h_j; the composite endpoint coincides with the actual flow endpoint (lime ✓).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Philip Hall coordinates h_j satisfy a differential equation driven by fictitious inputs v_j; differentiating the product formula introduces Ad-maps that are polynomial for nilpotent algebras.

atoms.idea: The h_j are Philip Hall coordinates: all reachable flows come from composing flows along basis elements — reminiscent of the product-of-exponentials formula for arms.
atoms.feynman: Like a robot arm’s pose being the product of each joint’s twist, any steering maneuver is a product of basis-move flows.
atoms.visual: Split view: a robot arm (orange joints, pink tip) built from POE next to the steering ribbon; both highlight segment-by-segment.

atoms.label: Eq (8.23)
atoms.idea: S(t) satisfies Ṡ = S(B1v1 + ⋯ + Bsvs), S(0) = 1, with fictitious inputs v_j along every basis direction; only the first m correspond to real inputs.
atoms.feynman: Pretend you have a knob for every move on the bookshelf, even the wiggle ones — later you will fake the extra knobs using real ones.
atoms.visual: Every book on the shelf gets a ghostly knob v_j (translucent orange for brackets, solid orange for g1, g2).

atoms.label: Eq (8.24)
atoms.idea: Differentiating the product gives Ṡ = Σ_j S · Ad_{e^{−h1B1}⋯e^{−h_{j−1}B_{j−1}}} ḣ_j B_j, with Ad_{e^{−hB}}B_j = e^{−hB} B_j e^{hB}.
atoms.feynman: Changing one move in the middle of a dance is like doing that move but "seen through" all the moves before it.
atoms.visual: Ribbon with one segment pulsing; its arrow is transported back through earlier segments (conjugation shown as the arrow rotating/tilting as it passes each segment).

atoms.label: Eq (8.25)
atoms.idea: Ad of a product is the product of Ads; nilpotency makes each a finite polynomial series, so each term equals Σ_k p_{j,k}(h) B_k ḣ_j.
atoms.feynman: Seen-through-many-moves = seen through one, then the next. Because wiggles stop after k levels, the result is a short list.
atoms.visual: Matrix of polynomial coefficients p_{j,k}(h) displayed as a triangular grid; most cells empty (zero) thanks to nilpotency.

atoms.idea: Matching coefficients of each B_k with (8.23): Σ_j p_{j,k}(h) ḣ_j = v_k.
atoms.feynman: Read off, book by book, how fast each coordinate must change to match the ghost knobs.
atoms.visual: Each shelf book lights when its equation balances: left-hand polynomial bar equals ghost knob v_k.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The Chen–Fliess–Sussmann equation ḣ = Q(h)v lives in s ≥ n dimensions; Example 8.5 works it out for a two-input, degree-three nilpotent system on R⁴.

atoms.label: Eq (8.26)
atoms.idea: Solving gives ḣ = Q(h)v, h(0) = 0, the Chen–Fliess–Sussmann equation: a control system in R^s (s can exceed n) that is the canonical form for the nilpotent algebra.
atoms.feynman: A bigger, simpler model toy that covers every possible version of your real machine; the real machine is a shadow of it.
atoms.visual: An s-dimensional bar panel of h_j values (teal), with a projection arrow down to the n-dimensional real state (blue).

atoms.label: Ex 8.5
atoms.idea: Two inputs, nilpotent of degree 3 on R⁴ with g1, g2, [g1,g2], [g1,[g1,g2]] independent. Basis B1 = g1, B2 = g2, B3 = [g1,g2], B4 = [g1,[g1,g2]], B5 = [g2,[g1,g2]] with v5 ≡ 0; coefficients of ḣ_j: B1; B2 − h1B3 + ½h1²B4; B3 − h2B5 − h1B4; B4; B5.
atoms.feynman: Four useful moves on the shelf plus one spare that duplicates the others, so its ghost knob is glued at zero.
atoms.visual: Shelf with five books, book B5 greyed with a 0-locked knob; the coefficient table appears row by row as polynomial chips.

atoms.idea: Example: Ad_{e^{−h1B1}}B2 = B2 − h1[B1,B2] + ½h1²[B1,[B1,B2]] = B2 − h1B3 + ½h1²B4.
atoms.feynman: Seeing g2 through a g1-move tilts it a bit into the wiggle direction, and a bit more into the wiggle-of-wiggle.
atoms.visual: Arrow B2 passes through a g1 segment of length h1 and picks up colored components along B3 (−h1) and B4 (½h1²); slider h1 shows them grow.

atoms.label: Eq (8.27)
atoms.idea: Result: ḣ1 = v1, ḣ2 = v2, ḣ3 = h1v2 + v3, ḣ4 = ½h1²v2 + h1v3 + v4, ḣ5 = h2v3 + h1h2v2.
atoms.feynman: A tidy chain-like toy model: a few counters each fed by simpler ones.
atoms.visual: Five teal h bars driven live by the ghost knobs v1…v4 using RK4; v5 slider locked at 0.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The canonical system lives in R⁵ although the state is in R⁴; Example 8.6 computes the Chen–Fliess–Sussmann coefficients for the five-state chain (nilpotent of degree 4).

atoms.idea: The canonical system evolves in R⁵ even though the real state space is R⁴.
atoms.feynman: The model toy has one extra dial that the real machine doesn’t show.
atoms.visual: Five bars vs four real readouts, with one bar ghosted in the projection.

atoms.label: Ex 8.6
atoms.idea: Five-state two-input chain (g1 = (1,0,q2,q3,q4), g2 = e2) is nilpotent of degree 4. Philip Hall basis: g1, g2; [g1,g2]; [g1,[g1,g2]], [g2,[g1,g2]]; three degree-4 brackets. g1, g2, ad g2, ad² g2, ad³ g2 span R⁵.
atoms.feynman: The five-trailer train: its bookshelf has eight moves, but only five of them actually point somewhere new.
atoms.visual: Bookshelf with 8 books on 4 shelves; 5 books glow lime (spanning), 3 grey (dependent); the chain-bead picture from the chained scene sits beside it.

atoms.idea: With v5 = v7 = v8 = 0, the coefficient of ḣ_j is the composed Ad of the earlier exponentials applied to B_j; e.g. for ḣ3: B3 − h1B4 − h2B5 + ½h1²B6 + h1h2B7 + ½h2²B8.
atoms.feynman: Look at move 3 through moves 1 and 2: it leaks into deeper wiggle directions by amounts that grow with how much of moves 1 and 2 you did.
atoms.visual: Arrow B3 passing through two segments (h1, h2) and collecting colored components on shelves 3 and 4 with polynomial magnitudes.

atoms.idea: The remaining coefficients follow the same way (left as a reader exercise).
atoms.feynman: Same trick for the rest — try it yourself.
atoms.visual: Remaining rows of the coefficient table appear with a "challenge" border; learner predicts each before reveal.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Full coefficient table and the eight-dimensional Chen–Fliess–Sussmann equation for the five-state chain; real inputs generate fictitious ones via bracket loops such as Eq (8.28).

atoms.idea: Coefficient table for ḣ1…ḣ8 (e.g. ḣ2: B2 − h1B3 + ½h1²B4 − ⅙h1³B6; ḣ4: B4 − h1B6 − h2B7; ḣ6…ḣ8: themselves).
atoms.feynman: The full answer key for "how does each move look after the earlier ones".
atoms.visual: Triangular table of polynomial chips; hover a chip to highlight its source segments on the ribbon.

atoms.idea: Resulting system in R⁸ with h(0) = 0: ḣ1 = v1, ḣ2 = v2, ḣ3 = h1v2 + v3, ḣ4 = ½h1²v2 + h1v3 + v4, ḣ5 = h1h2v2 + h2v3, ḣ6 = ⅙h1³v2 + ½h1²v3 + h1v4 + v6, ḣ7 = ½h1²h2v2 + h1h2v3 + h2v4, ḣ8 = ½h1h2²v2 + ½h2²v3.
atoms.feynman: An eight-counter abacus where each counter is fed by polynomials of the earlier ones — still just bookkeeping.
atoms.visual: Eight h bars driven by ghost knobs (v5, v7, v8 locked at 0); live RK4 integration.

atoms.idea: To steer: pick any path from q0 to qf, plug it into (8.23) to read off fictitious inputs along the first n independent basis directions, then realize those using the real inputs — which needs a generalized bracket construction.
atoms.feynman: Draw the route you wish you could drive (even sideways), work out which ghost knobs it needs, then fake each ghost knob with real wiggles.
atoms.visual: Gold straight-line wish path; a panel shows required ghost-knob signals v_j(t); each ghost knob gets replaced by a small orange loop icon of real-input switches.

atoms.label: Eq (8.28)
atoms.idea: For v3 (direction [g1,g2]) use four segments of √ε seconds: (u1,u2) = (1,0), (0,1), (−1,0), (0,−1); the flow is e^{√ε g1}e^{√ε g2}e^{−√ε g1}e^{−√ε g2}.
atoms.feynman: East, north, west, south: you come back nearly to start, shifted by the "wiggle" direction an amount equal to the square’s area.
atoms.visual: Blue cart traces a square of side √ε with orange segments; the net displacement arrow (gold) lies along [g1,g2] with length ε; side slider shows displacement scales as side².

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The Campbell–Baker–Hausdorff formula (Thm 8.5) explains what a box loop produces; nilpotency makes it exact; without nilpotency the method only approximates.

atoms.label: Thm 8.5, Eq (8.29)
atoms.idea: CBH: e^{g1}e^{g2} = exp(g1 + g2 + ½[g1,g2] + (1/12)([g1,[g1,g2]] − [g2,[g1,g2]]) + ⋯), further terms by matching formal power series.
atoms.feynman: Doing move A then move B is like doing A and B blended together, plus half a wiggle, plus a tiny wiggle-of-wiggle correction, and so on.
atoms.visual: Two flow arrows composed (orange then orange) vs a single blended arrow plus correction arrows (teal ½ bracket, smaller purple 1/12 terms); a toggle adds terms and the endpoints converge (lime).

atoms.idea: Applying CBH to the box loop gives h = (0, 0, ε, h4(ε)) with h4 higher order: the loop moves along [g1,g2] but also leaks into [g1,[g1,g2]], while h1, h2 stay put. An eight-segment loop with ∛ε pieces targets the deeper direction; nilpotency makes the series finite, so the construction is exact and generalizes.
atoms.feynman: Your square parking wiggle mostly slides you sideways but also twists you slightly; a bigger, two-level wiggle fixes the twist. Since the toy has finitely many hidden directions, a finite set of wiggles does it exactly.
atoms.visual: Box loop leaves a gold arrow (ε, along shelf 2) plus a small purple leak arrow on shelf 3. Switch to the eight-leg loop (∛ε): the shelf-2 arrow vanishes and a clean shelf-3 arrow appears.

atoms.idea: Without nilpotency the algorithm only steers approximately: the Philip Hall basis is infinite and the CBH series doesn’t terminate.
atoms.feynman: If every wiggle reveals a new hidden direction forever, you can’t list them all — you can only get closer and closer.
atoms.visual: Bookshelf grows endless shelves fading upward; CBH term counter keeps climbing (∞ icon in purple).

atoms.idea: Remedies: transform inputs with a matrix β so the new fields g̃ = β g form a nilpotent system, or use nilpotent approximations of the system; see Lafferriere–Sussmann for details.
atoms.feynman: Mix your knobs into new combos that behave like the finite toy, or pretend your machine is the toy and fix errors by repeating.
atoms.visual: Input-mixing matrix sliders β; a nilpotency meter shows higher shelves emptying for good choices; repeated passes halve the coral distance to gold.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: A three-fingered hand (Fig 8.2) motivates repositioning fingertips by rolling; the grasp constraint J_h θ̇ = Gᵀẋ splits into object motion and internal (null-space) finger motion.

atoms.label: Fig 8.2
atoms.idea: A three-fingered hand grasping an ellipsoidal object; small circles under each finger depict the internal squeezing forces.
atoms.feynman: Holding an egg with three fingers: each finger pushes inward a little so the egg doesn’t drop, and the pushes cancel each other.
atoms.visual: 3D: slate ellipsoid held by three fingers (orange joints, pink tips); under each finger a small purple circle sized by its internal force; forces sum to zero (lime readout).

atoms.idea: Section 8.4 Dynamic finger repositioning.
Goal: move fingertips over the object without lifting them, by pure rolling of spherical fingertips on flat faces (Chapter 7 showed this is possible); several solutions follow.
atoms.feynman: Shift your grip on a ball by rolling your fingertips over it instead of letting go.
atoms.visual: One pink fingertip ball rolls along a slate box face, leaving a teal contact trail; the box never drops (contact lock icon lime).

atoms.idea: Section 8.4.1 Problem description.

atoms.label: Eq (8.30)
atoms.idea: Rolling-contact grasp constraints (from Chapter 5) in local coordinates: J_h(θ,x)θ̇ = Gᵀ(θ,x)ẋ, θ finger joints, x object pose.
atoms.feynman: The fingertips must move exactly as the object surface moves under them — like hands on a steering wheel.
atoms.visual: Joint-speed arrows (orange) mapped by J_h and object-speed arrows (blue) mapped by Gᵀ meet at teal contact points; a balance readout shows both sides equal.

atoms.idea: If the grasp is manipulable, any object velocity is achievable; when J_h has a null space, finger velocities are not unique — internal motions leave the object still. Let u1 drive the object and u2 parameterize internal motions.
atoms.feynman: Your fingers can shuffle around a mug you’re holding still — there are extra ways to move that the mug doesn’t feel.
atoms.visual: Null-space slider (orange) wiggles the fingers while the object stays perfectly still (object velocity readout = 0, lime); a second slider moves the object.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Grasp kinematics as a control system (Eq 8.31); the redundant case lets fingers move with the object fixed, reducing to one sphere-tipped finger rolling on a plane (Eq 8.32).

atoms.label: Eq (8.31)
atoms.idea: Control form: ẋ = u1, θ̇ = J_h⁺Gᵀu1 + Ku2, with columns of K spanning null(J_h).
atoms.feynman: One knob moves the held object; the other only reshuffles the fingers.
atoms.visual: Two orange knobs: u1 moves the slate object and the fingers follow; u2 moves fingers along null-space directions (purple arrows) with object fixed.

atoms.idea: Dynamic finger repositioning: steer (θ0,x0) to (θf,xf); fingertip contact locations follow from forward kinematics.
atoms.feynman: Start holding the cup one way and end holding it another way, without letting go.
atoms.visual: Ghost start grasp (translucent) and gold goal grasp; contact points computed live from joint angles.

atoms.idea: General case is hard. Special cases: (1) no redundancy — only object motion u1, and moving contacts needs a closed loop in x; (2) redundancy — move fingers with ẋ = u1 = 0 using only K directions; then fingers decouple and one finger suffices. The second case is studied.
atoms.feynman: Either juggle the cup in a little circle so it rolls under your fingers, or keep it still and let each finger walk on its own.
atoms.visual: Toggle: case 1 shows the object tracing a small closed loop while contacts creep; case 2 freezes the object and isolates one finger with a spotlight.

atoms.idea: Section 8.4.2 Steering using sinusoids.

atoms.label: Eq (8.32)
atoms.idea: One spherical finger rolling on a plane: η̇ = (0, sec q1, −sin q5, −cos q5, −tan q1)u1 + (−1, 0, −cos q5, sin q5, 0)u2, with q1,q2 the contact on the finger, q3,q4 on the plane, q5 the contact angle.
atoms.feynman: Roll a marble under your palm: two ways to roll it, but five things change — where on the marble, where on the table, and how it’s twisted.
atoms.visual: Ball on table with five readouts (two pink finger-contact coords, two teal table coords, one orange twist angle); two orange roll knobs.

atoms.idea: Change of state: z1 = q1, z2 = q2, z3 = −q5, z4 = q3 − q1, z5 = q4 + q2, tracking Taylor terms to obtain a two-chain.
atoms.feynman: Relabel the five readouts so they line up as two short trailer chains.
atoms.visual: Five readouts slide into two bead chains (z1→z3→… and z2→…), labeled by color.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Fig 8.3: sinusoidal steering slides a ball fingertip down an object face while the finger contact loops back; with v = (−u2, sec q1 u1), the rolling system is a two-chain plus higher-order terms.

atoms.label: Fig 8.3
atoms.idea: Multifingered hand on a box: finger-contact coordinates (u_f, v_f) trace a closed figure-eight while object-contact coordinates (u_o, v_o) trace a loop that ends displaced downward.
atoms.feynman: Walking a fingertip down a box by rocking it: the spot on your finger goes around and returns, but the spot on the box ends up lower.
atoms.visual: Two live plots: pink (u_f,v_f) figure-eight closing on itself; teal (u_o,v_o) curve whose end is below its start (gold marker); 3D hand on box on the left.

atoms.label: Eq (8.33)
atoms.idea: With v1 = −u2, v2 = sec q1 u1: ż1 = v1, ż2 = v2, ż3 = z1v2 + ψ1, ż4 = z3v2 + …, ż5 = z3v1 + …, where ψ_i are quadratic or higher; dropping them leaves a two-chain steerable by sinusoids.
atoms.feynman: Up close (small rolls), the marble behaves exactly like two little trailer chains; the leftovers are tiny.
atoms.visual: Two-chain bead diagram; coral "ψ" leftover arrows on beads 3–5 shrink as the roll amplitude slider decreases.

atoms.idea: Unlike the hopper or car, the Fourier coefficients for z4, z5 are hard to get in closed form, so a numerical search over integer-frequency sines/cosines steers the finger; Fig 8.3 shows a path down an object side.
atoms.feynman: When you can’t compute the right wiggle by hand, try wiggles and adjust their sizes until it works.
atoms.visual: Coefficient sliders for sin/cos at 1× and 2×; a solver nudges them until the teal endpoint hits the gold mark on the face.

atoms.idea: In the figure, the finger contact (q1,q2) returns to its start while the object contact (q3,q4) shifts in the v_o direction.
atoms.feynman: Same spot on your fingertip, new spot on the box.
atoms.visual: Pink loop closes (lime ✓ on finger contact), teal endpoint offset arrow along v_o (gold).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Geometric phase: for a sphere rolling on a plane, the contact angle changes at rate −sin u_f · v̇_f, independent of radius; Gauss–Bonnet gives Δψ = −(enclosed area).

atoms.idea: Section 8.4.3 Geometric phase algorithm.
Classical differential geometry gives a direct method for rolling a spherical finger on a plane.
atoms.feynman: Old geometry from map-makers turns out to solve the finger-rolling puzzle.
atoms.visual: Globe with latitude/longitude grid next to a flat table.
atoms.beat: 🌐 roll a ball on the table

atoms.label: Eq (8.34)
atoms.idea: Contact configuration η = (α_f, α_o, ψ): local coordinates on finger and object surfaces plus the contact angle. Rolling without slipping: M_f α̇_f − R_ψ M_o α̇_o = 0 and T_f M_f α̇_f + T_o M_o α̇_o − ψ̇ = 0.
atoms.feynman: Two surfaces touching and rolling: the contact spot moves the same distance on both, and the twist follows from how the surfaces curve.
atoms.visual: Ball on table: pink contact trail on the ball and teal trail on the table always equal length (two length readouts match); orange twist dial ψ.
atoms.beat: 🌐 roll a ball on the table

atoms.idea: Sphere of radius ρ on a plane: M_o = I, T_o = 0, M_f = diag(ρ, ρ cos u_f), T_f = (0, −tan u_f / ρ).
atoms.feynman: On a globe, moving one degree east covers less ground near the poles (cos of latitude); the table is flat so nothing changes there.
atoms.visual: Globe grid cells shrinking toward the poles; a cos u_f bar beside the latitude slider.
atoms.beat: 🌐 roll a ball on the table

atoms.label: Eq (8.35)
atoms.idea: Since M_f, R_ψ M_o are invertible, any finger path α_f(t) lifts uniquely to a contact path: α̇_f = u, α̇_o = M_o⁻¹R_ψ M_f u, ψ̇ = (T_f + T_o R_ψ)M_f u — a lifting map from S_f to Q.
atoms.feynman: Decide how the spot moves on the ball, and the table spot and twist are completely determined.
atoms.visual: Draw a pink path on the ball with the mouse; the teal table path and the orange twist dial are computed live.
atoms.beat: 🌐 roll a ball on the table

atoms.label: Eq (8.36)
atoms.idea: For sphere on plane: ψ̇ = −sin u_f · u2 (u2 = v̇_f), independent of the radius ρ, so results for the unit sphere hold for all radii.
atoms.feynman: How much the ball twists depends only on the angles you roll through, not on how big the ball is.
atoms.visual: Radius slider changes the ball’s size; the twist readout for the same angular path does not change (lime).

atoms.label: Thm 8.6, Eq (8.37)
atoms.idea: Gauss–Bonnet: if the finger path is a closed curve on the unit sphere enclosing a cap Ω, rolling along it changes the contact angle by Δψ = −Area(Ω).
atoms.feynman: Carry a pencil around a closed loop on a globe without ever turning it relative to the surface: when you return, it points in a new direction, and the turn equals the area you circled.
atoms.visual: Draw a closed pink loop on the ball; the enclosed cap fills gold; area readout and twist readout show equal magnitudes (opposite sign).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Proof via Green’s theorem that the phase equals minus the enclosed spherical area; geometric phase is radius independent; Prop 8.7 starts a planar recipe for moving the contact point.

atoms.label: Fig 8.4
atoms.idea: A closed path α_f(t) on a sphere bounding a cap Ω.
atoms.feynman: A loop drawn around the top of an orange: the peel inside is the area.
atoms.visual: 3D unit sphere with a pink loop near the north pole and the gold cap Ω shaded.

atoms.idea: The area is measured on the curved unit sphere.
atoms.feynman: Measure the peel, not its flat shadow.
atoms.visual: Toggle between the curved cap and its flat projection; only the curved area matches the twist.
